messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 72

# A Matter of Seconds

Marcus sits in the waiting room with his hands folded tightly in his lap, the familiar knot of tension already forming in his chest before the session even begins. At forty-two, he still carries himself with the careful posture of someone accustomed to precision—the same meticulous attention to detail that has served him well during his twenty years as a tax inspector. But lately, that precision feels like a liability, a cruel reminder of how much he cannot control.

The incident happened fourteen months ago on a Saturday morning in late spring. Marcus had been backing his car out of the driveway while his wife, Priya, was inside the house. Their neighbor's seven-year-old son, Rohan, had been playing near the property line—something Marcus hadn't seen in his side mirror. The sound of the impact is something he cannot unhear. It wasn't loud, exactly. It was definitive. Final. In the seconds that followed, Marcus's mind fractured into a before and an after.

Rohan survived. He spent three weeks in the hospital with a fractured femur, internal bleeding, and a concussion that caused seizures for several days. The guilt that Marcus carries is not proportional to the outcome—he knows this intellectually, the way he knows tax codes and audit procedures. But knowledge and feeling exist in different rooms in his mind, and they rarely speak to each other anymore.

For the first few months, Marcus continued going to work. He would sit at his desk in the revenue office, reviewing financial documents with the same careful eye he'd always employed, but the numbers would blur and separate. He'd find himself staring at a spreadsheet for forty minutes without processing a single figure. His supervisor eventually suggested he take medical leave. By then, Marcus was already sleeping only two or three hours per night, his mind replaying the moment in endless variation—sometimes he sees Rohan in time, sometimes he doesn't, and in those versions where he doesn't, the outcomes are always worse.

The hypervigilance has colonized every aspect of his life. When he drives now, which he does only when absolutely necessary, his hands grip the wheel so tightly they ache for hours afterward. He checks his mirrors obsessively, sometimes five or six times in a single block. Last month, he nearly caused an accident when he swerved to avoid what he thought was a child in the road—it was a plastic bag. Priya has stopped asking him to drive. She's stopped asking him to do many things.

At night, when he does sleep, the dreams come with a vividness that feels almost hallucinatory. He dreams of the impact, of blood on asphalt, of Rohan's mother's face when she came running. He wakes gasping, his heart rate elevated enough that he has to sit on the edge of the bed and count his breaths until the room stops spinning. Priya lies beside him, pretending to sleep, and Marcus knows she's awake because her breathing is wrong.

He's withdrawn from friends, from the temple community where he and Priya have been active for years, from the small rituals that once structured his life. The guilt feels like a living thing—something that feeds on his attention and grows larger the more he examines it. He replays his own negligence in forensic detail: he should have checked twice, should have waited, should have been more careful. The word "should" has become the dominant feature of his internal landscape.

Marcus knows that Rohan is recovering well, that the boy's parents have forgiven him, that the accident was exactly that—an accident. But knowing and believing are different currencies, and right now, he's bankrupt in the latter.
